Pursue means to go after something — with intention, effort, and persistence over time.

The "going after" can be physical (chasing someone down a street) or it can be mental and emotional (spending years working toward a dream). Both are correct uses of the same word.

The three invisible qualities hidden inside "pursue" are:

  • Direction — you are moving toward something specific
  • Effort — it requires active doing, not passive waiting
  • Continuity — it happens over a period of time, not in a single instant

1. To physically chase or follow someone or something

This is the most literal, visual sense of the word. One thing moves, and you go after it.

The police pursued the suspect through the alley.
The lioness pursued the zebra across the open field.

Here, "pursue" and "chase" are nearly identical. The difference is subtle: "chase" feels more urgent and short-lived, while "pursue" can suggest a longer, more determined effort.

2. To work toward a goal, dream, or ambition

This is the most common and important meaning you will encounter. When someone "pursues" a dream, a career, or success, it means they are consistently putting in effort over time to reach it.

She pursued her dream of becoming a surgeon for over a decade.
He left his home country to pursue a better life.
They pursued excellence in everything they did.

Notice that this meaning lives entirely in the mind and in action — there is no physical chasing involved. Yet it perfectly fits the word because the core idea is still: going after something intentionally, with effort, over time.

3. To continue doing an activity, study, or interest

When you "pursue" a subject or activity, you are actively engaging in it on an ongoing basis — it is something you keep coming back to and developing.

After retiring, he pursued painting as a serious hobby.
The university encouraged her to pursue research in climate science.
She pursued her studies even while working two jobs.

The key here is the word ongoing. You don't "pursue" something you did once. You pursue something you dedicate time and energy to, repeatedly.

4. To keep investigating, discussing, or following up on something

In conversations, meetings, or professional life, "pursue" means to take something further — to not let it drop, but to keep pushing on it.

The detective pursued every lead until she found the truth.
The journalist pursued the story for six months before publishing.
I don't want to pursue this argument any further tonight.
The company decided not to pursue the matter in court.

Here, "pursue" is about sustained attention — you are actively following something through, rather than leaving it unfinished.

5. To seek someone's romantic attention

When a person "pursues" another person romantically, it means they are making persistent, deliberate efforts to attract or win that person's affection.

He had been pursuing her for months before she agreed to a date.
She wasn't interested in being pursued by anyone at that point in her life.
The One Thread That Ties All Meanings Together

No matter which situation you use it in, pursue always carries the same DNA:

Something exists that you want → you move toward it → you keep at it → it takes time and effort.

Whether it is a thief running away, a lifelong dream, a research project, a romantic interest, or an unresolved conversation — the word "pursue" fits whenever that formula applies.

• It is not a one-time action. You don't "pursue" something you did once by accident. The word implies sustained, deliberate effort.
  • It is not passive. You cannot pursue something while sitting still and waiting. Pursuing requires you to actively move toward the thing.
  • It is not the same as "reach" or "achieve." Pursuing is the journey. You pursue a goal; you achieve it (or don't) later.
A Useful Way to Remember It

Think of the word pursue as carrying a built-in image: a person walking steadily forward, eyes fixed on something in the distance, not giving up.

That image — steady, intentional, forward-moving, not stopping — is what the word means in every context it is used.

• pursue a dream / goal / passion / ambition
  • pursue a career / education / degree
  • pursue a matter / case / lead / story
  • pursue someone (romantically or in a chase)
  • pursue happiness / freedom / truth
  • actively / aggressively / relentlessly / vigorously pursue

The word pairs naturally with things that are worth going after and that require sustained effort to reach.
